In fact it is a very different thing whether we have to do with a work of art or a copy of nature, as if the work of art were nothing more than a mere likeness of what exists.

but these shapes must, however, be treated in a manner appropriate to the spiritual, so that the natural shall be in it subordinated to the spiritual and transformed into a spiritual shape. This transformation of the natural, which, as such, is the mere given, into a spiritual form, is the work of art.

and it is the task of the artist to find such forms and to make them his own. But the end is the making of them his own; and he can do this only in so far as the spiritual content is the principal thing, and the natural is only the matter which the spirit takes up into itself and makes its own.

continuation.opening: Their particularity becomes more and more fixed and ossified. Unity of the body is essential to health, and where the organs become hard death ensues. Everlasting peace is frequently demanded as the ideal towards which mankind must move. Hence, Kant proposed an alliance of princes, which should settle the controversies of states, and the Holy Alliance was probably intended to be an institution of this kind.
continuation.rest: But the state is individual, and in individuality negation is essentially implied. Although a number of states may make themselves into a family, the union, because it is an individuality, must create an opposition, and so beget an enemy. As a result of war peoples are strengthened, nations, which are involved in civil quarrels, winning repose at home by means of war abroad.
answers: But such a peace, if it is to last, must be based on the fact that no one has any complaint to make; it is in its nature a deathlike peace; it is a peace at the price of the individual's life and freedom. The living movement of the world lies in the fact that individuality should assert itself against the universal, and that the latter should, as its life, recognize individuality and give it the power of action.

But the alliance of princes is a very arbitrary and unstable body; the state is a living rational entity, and so is the universal ethical order. Hence it would be as ridiculous to desire the extinction of war as it would be to demand that nature should cease to work; war is a means by which the states maintain their ethical self-consciousness and the nations their independence as ethical individuals.

But it is absurd to expect that states, which have been the theatre of so many contentions and whose national existence depends on their mutual relations, should be able to enter into such a union. It is as if men were to be required to be bound by the laws of a single commonwealth and to give up the freedom of action which is essential to the life of the body.

But this peace is the peace of the dead, not the peace of the living. The living, on the contrary, require the development of a healthy state. In the latter, as in the body, there is a constant circulation of the blood, and it is the vital activity of the blood which preserves the body in health, and is the very condition of health.

continuation.opening: Love is in general the consciousness of the unity of myself with another. I am not separate and isolated, but win my self-consciousness only by renouncing my independent existence, and by knowing myself as unity of myself with another and of another with me.
continuation.rest: But love is feeling, that is to say, the ethical in the form of the natural. It has no longer a place in the state, where one knows the unity as law, where, too, the content must be rational, and I must know it.
answers: In the family this unity is actual and immediate. In ethical love there is a real and complete unity; in sensuous love, insofar as it is a mere impulse, there is not a unity of the free individuality, but only of the single individual with himself in the form of the other.
This is love. I am not the other, but I know myself to be the other, and the other knows himself to be me. This unity is the true existence of both, and for this reason it is the truth of each.

This unity in its immediate form is sensuous, in the form of the mutual enjoyment of love; and since in this enjoyment it is the other who is the object, love is in its immediate form a passion, an impulse, a feeling.
But this is the very essence of the Spirit. It is the Spirit which in the first place creates the unity of myself and another, and at the same time is the product of that unity.

continuation.opening: As the substance, being an intelligent substance, particularises itself abstractly into many persons (the family is only a single person), into families or individuals, who exist independent and free, as private persons, it loses its ethical character:
continuation.rest: for these persons as such have in their consciousness and as their aim not the absolute unity, but their own petty selves and particular interests. Thus arises the system of atomistic: by which the substance is reduced to a general system of adjustments to connect self-subsisting extremes and their particular interests.
answers: and in so far as it exists thus, it is civil society. This, the second form of ethical life, is the ethical bond, but in the form of a natural bond, in which freedom is, as it were, only as a moment.

for the family is ethical, but the individuals are not. Hence the second form of the ethical, the civil state, which is the sphere of independence, and the principle of which is the distinction of persons, each of whom has in itself an end, and is a complete person.

for in this character individuals do not stand as independent individuals, but in the form of ethical unity. It is in the abstract individuality of this ethical form that the individual exists in the ethical world; and it is in the form of this abstract individuality that he is a person and a member of the family.

for the ethical person is an end in itself, and is free only as such. The particular persons are thus opposed to one another; and each one is an independent end, an independent unity of being-for-self and for-others. These are the two moments of personality; but the person is the unity of both, and is not one or the other alone.

continuation.opening: The hollow object, which it produces, now fills it, therefore, with the feeling of emptiness. Its activity consists in yearning; it merely loses itself in becoming an unsubstantial shadowy object, and, rising above this loss and falling back on itself, finds itself merely as lost.
continuation.rest: In this transparent purity of its moments it becomes a sorrow-laden "beautiful soul," as it is called; its light dims and dies within it, and it vanishes as a shapeless vapour dissolving into thin air.
answers: Its life is the mere life of self-relinquishment. In its own being, in its own activity and its own production, it does not find itself.

It is as if in the course of a dream, when a person imagines himself to be flying, and is thereby only the more conscious of the fact that he is sitting in a chair and that he is flying only in his dreams.

It is not satisfied in itself; its self-satisfaction is rather to be satisfied in another. Its aim is to find its own self in otherness. This is the yearning of the beautiful soul, and in this lies its beauty.
In this manner it is the pure movement of the feeling of the loss of the feeling of loss, and in this infinite, restless movement it has the certainty that it is a good being.

continuation.opening: If we go on to cast a look at the fate of these World-Historical persons, whose vocation it was to be the agents of the World-Spirit,—we shall find it to have been no happy one. They attained no calm enjoyment;
continuation.rest: their whole life was labour and trouble; their whole nature was nought else but their master-passion. When their object is attained they fall off like empty hulls from the kernel. They die early, like Alexander; they are murdered, like Caesar; transported to St. Helena, like Napoleon.
answers: their own particular interests were neglected, and in most cases their existence was broken off in the midst of their career; and, after all, there remains to them no other consolation, than the satisfaction of feeling that they have fulfilled the business in question.

they were for the most part the victims of the very world which they have produced. Alexander died young; Caesar was stabbed, and the Roman Empire which he founded, did not fall to the hands of his family.

they were torn by passions; the evil which they worked,—and it is the characteristic of the World-Historical person, that he must not be allowed to remain within the limits of the good,—that he must make a breach in the existing state of things,—has brought upon him a heavy burden of guilt.

the most brilliant of them were either in their lifetime or after their death the objects of reproach, and the subjects of many a slander. If Alexander had been spared to enjoy the fruit of his toils, he would have fallen a victim to the poison-cup.

continuation.opening: Here there is a self-consciousness for a self-consciousness, at first immediately as one of two things for another. In that other as ego I behold myself, and yet also an immediately existing object, another ego absolutely independent of me and opposed to me.
continuation.rest: (The suppression of the singleness of self-consciousness was only a first step in the suppression, and it merely led to the characterisation of it as particular.) This contradiction gives either self-consciousness the impulse to show itself as a free self, and to exist as such for the other:—the process of recognition.
answers: This other is at first for me not an absolute self, but merely an object. The fact that I am independent of it as of an object does not yet in the first place mean that I am the self, the absolute being; I have not yet passed beyond the immediate being of the other.

I am self-consciousness only in so far as I am the object for another self-consciousness; but I am not so in the form of immediacy, but as another self-consciousness which is for me self-consciousness, just as I am for it. In order to be certain of its existence, self-consciousness must therefore be able to bring about an alteration in another self-consciousness.

But the ego of this other is also essentially for itself. Here, therefore, we have a situation where two opposite forces are in operation, and the opposition is not something static but dynamic. Each of the two is not a thing but a living self.

The self-consciousness, which is for another, is not for itself a universal self-consciousness; it is only, like a thing, the singular self-consciousness of the other, and therefore this is its object. But this object is not a thing; it is another self-consciousness.

continuation.opening: Only one word more concerning the desire to teach the world what it ought to be. For such a purpose philosophy at least always comes too late. Philosophy, as the thought of the world, does not appear until reality has completed its formative process, and made itself ready.
continuation.rest: History thus corroborates the teaching of the conception that only in the maturity of reality does the ideal appear as counterpart to the real, apprehends the real world in its substance, and shapes it into an intellectual kingdom. When philosophy paints its grey in grey, one form of life has become old, and by means of grey it cannot be rejuvenated, but only known. The owl of Minerva takes its flight only when the shades of night are gathering.
answers: This thought, when it comes to maturity, can only depict its own reality. From the standpoint of theory, it is impossible for us to anticipate the world and arrive at what is to come. Even if philosophy were to attempt it, she would not be able to make it known before its time. This is because her work is the understanding of what is, and this is in the same way the truth.

The concept which comes only after the fact, and which is therefore at once the concept of that which has been, cannot alter the course of things any more. But the moment it has attained completeness, the actuality, on the other hand, has entered its phase of dissolution, and thus, instead of its being philosophy that adapts reality to itself, it is reality rather which adapts itself to philosophy. This is the strange relation which the concept of right bears to the world of right.

In its grey in-grey, the thought can only depict the grey of the existing. When philosophy paints the grey of the real in grey, it is also the sign that something new is about to be born. However, the grey of the concept cannot make itself beautiful for the day to come, but can only understand and represent it. In the light of that grey, one age has passed away and a new one has dawned.

As thought, it can only depict reality after its completion; and in this way, in the grey in the grey of philosophy, the old form of life becomes grey. It is not possible for the same grey to make the new one young. Philosophy can, at the point of time when the spirit has outgrown it, describe the consciousness of a previous age; but it cannot prescribe what should come after. With that, philosophy has done.

continuation.opening: To apprehend what is is the task of philosophy, because what is is reason. As for the individual, every one is a son of his time; so philosophy also is its time apprehended in thoughts.
continuation.rest: It is just as foolish to fancy that any philosophy can transcend its present world, as that an individual could leap out of his time or jump over Rhodes. If a theory transgresses its time, and builds up a world as it ought to be, it has an existence merely in the unstable element of opinion, which gives room to every wandering fancy.
answers: This saying contains the thought that philosophy like every other product of thought, being something finite, cannot be older than its time, that is the actuality in which it lives. It cannot be older in the same sense as it may be younger. It is not a mere recollection or memorial of things past, for that would be of no use to the present.

Therefore just as one may not expect that philosophy will raise a people above its time, so one may expect that philosophy will not raise itself above its own. Philosophy cannot tell the world what it ought to be, for it deals with what is and its necessity; and only when it is already there in reality, the new appears.

Just as a portrait of a god does not thereby make the god itself, so philosophy also does not bring philosophy to existence, but simply represents it. The philosophy of a period is that period in its essence. The grey of the owl spreads its wings only when the dusk of the day is falling.

The philosophy of any particular epoch can, therefore, never be in advance of the epoch, but, in the same manner as its world, can never be in advance of its time; for the real is the whole, and in the whole reason exists as actual. If, before its time, a philosophy appears to be in advance, this is because it is in fact a philosophy of a previous time.

continuation.opening: A person must give to his freedom an external sphere, in order that he may reach the completeness implied in the idea. Since a person is as yet the first abstract phase of the completely existent, infinite will, the external sphere of freedom is not only distinguishable from him but directly different and separable.
continuation.rest: The reasonableness of property consists not in its satisfying our needs, but in its superseding and replacing the subjective phase of personality. It is in possession first of all that the person becomes rational. The first realization of my freedom in an external object is an imperfect one, it is true, but it is the only realization possible so long as the abstract personality has this first-hand relation to its object.
answers: The person is a negative power with regard to it, and in its sphere he has his reality. This external sphere is the possession, property [das Eigenthum] of a person. The property [das Eigenthum] is an expression of the will; the will is a will that has become real in an object, and its reality is the property [das Eigenthum] of a person.

The external sphere of freedom is property, i.e. something that can become mine. In order to make the whole of my person free, I must externalise the abstract idea of the will in a sphere that is not the will but has its existence in a form outside me. It is not the purpose of property to satisfy my wants, my inclinations, and desires. Property is the embodiment of personality.

This is the external object or external world. The sphere of external objects is, in fact, the objectification of freedom itself, and it has the significance of being the embodiment of freedom, as an external world distinct from the person. The person is thereby set in relation to something that is not his own, and he is thereby limited by this other.
He must give to his freedom an external sphere, but the external sphere is something other than the person.

continuation.opening: The injury which the criminal experiences is inherently just because it expresses his own inherent will, is a visible proof of his freedom and is his right. But more than that, the injury is a right of the criminal himself, and is implied in his realized will or act.
continuation.rest: In his act, the act of a rational being, is involved a universal element, which by the act is set up as a law. This law he has recognized in his act, and has consented to be placed under it as under his right.
answers: In the first place, punishment is the right of the criminal, in so far as he himself has determined his act. The act, and the punishment which is its result, are both the work of the criminal. If the act is his own, he is equally his own punisher.

For the criminal is a rational being and it is his inherent will or rational will that he should have a right and that his acts should be recognized as his free acts. In punishing the criminal, his right is acknowledged and he is himself treated as a person.
Injury has to be inflicted on him in so far as he is a person; but if this is what it is, and if he is a person, he himself must will it.
For the act, as such, is a nullity, and the negation of this nullity is a double negation, or the negation of the nullity of his own act; so that the punishment is his own act.

continuation.opening: It is easy for one to grasp the notion that the state is the self-determining and completely sovereign will, whose judgment is final. It is more difficult to apprehend this "I will" as a person. By this is not meant that the monarch can be wilful in his acts.
continuation.rest: Rather is he bound to the concrete content of the advice of his councillors, and, when the constitution is established, he has often nothing to do but sign his name. But this name is weighty. It is the summit, over which nothing can climb.
answers: It is not a matter of his choosing what he wills to do; his choice has to do with what is right. The monarch's decision is the last stage in the formation of the act of the state, inasmuch as the act of the state is only in its completion actual.

On the contrary, in the state the monarch is the least individual of individuals. The will of the state is the state. The monarch is the monarch only in so far as he is the monarch of the state, and the state is the monarch only in so far as it is the will of the sovereign.

For he is to be regarded as the living embodiment of the national spirit, and is a person as this spirit, i.e. the state, is a person. It is in the monarch that the state has its subjective or personal existence.
His will must be a rational one, for the rationality of the state lies in the fact that it is a union of the ethical powers which make up the rational whole.

continuation.opening: The German Spirit is the Spirit of the new World. Its aim is the realization of absolute Truth as the unlimited self-determination of Freedom—that Freedom which has its own absolute form itself as its purport. The destiny of the German peoples is, to be the bearers of the Christian principle.
continuation.rest: The principle of Spiritual Freedom—of Reconciliation [of the Objective and Subjective],was introduced into the still simple, unformed minds of those peoples; and the part assigned them in the service of the World-Spirit was that of not merely possessing the Idea of Freedom as the substratum of their religious conceptions, but of producing it in free and spontaneous developments from their subjective self-consciousness.
answers: The German Spirit, in the development of the Christian principle, is the Spirit of the new World. Its aim is the realization of absolute Truth, as the unlimited self-determination of Freedom—that Freedom which has its own absolute form itself as its purport. The destiny of the German peoples is, to be the bearers of the Christian principle.

They have received the new principle of Christianity and developed it; but they have not yet developed it in a fully rational form, in accordance with the true nature of Spirit; they are still in the middle of the process of development; the highest stage is not yet reached.

The Spirit of the Greek world had for its aim, the formation of the human being; the Roman, the formation of the State; the Teutonic, the formation of the Christian man, in the free community of love. The German peoples are therefore the bearers of the third form of the Spirit, the Spirit of the new World.

The Christian principle has been for centuries the basis of the European nations, but it was not so among the Greeks. In the German World, however, it has come to be a positive, effective force, and has been realized in the whole sphere of life.
